chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 15 of 21), named for no shrine: most confess bondage to courtesans who seek money and ask for the feet, knowledge or release; others ask to be freed from the round of wombs, picture the corpse carried to the pyre and Yama's summons, and offer a garland of letters; a long litany of the Goddess, Sambandar's impaling of the Jains and Kannappar's offering appear in the praise.
structure_note: Courtesan and lovemaking songs (1202, 1206 to 1208, 1210, 1213, 1214, 1216); the corpse and death (1203, 1204, 1215); rebirth (1205); self-abuse and the plea for non-dual knowledge (1209, 1211); a song offered as a garland (1212).

1202.reading: The poet describes women whose eyes are Kama's arrows, arms bamboo, breasts hills and hair darker than clouds, and asks that he no longer stand again and again in the houses of the deceitful-hearted, but that his mind come near Murugan's flawless feet with joy and love. The praise has Vishnu who measured the earth, the vel that split the hill and the mango and shook the serpents' world, Siva who drank the poison and dances with his consort, and Murugan who says 'fear not' in danger to the devotees who stand in justice.
1202.nuance: வஞ்ச நெஞ்சர் கூடத்தில் நின்று நின்று: the repeated நின்று gives the poet's loitering at the women's doors.

1203.reading: The poet takes the corpse of one ruined by offence, whom all mock with 'chi, chi' while even the four bearers laugh and which burns to nothing in the fire, and asks that in the same way his impurities, with the two diseases and the Kali age, die, so that he becomes pure space and Murugan comes on the peacock to give release. The praise names Siva of the Ganga and the bull who laughed the three cities to husk and burned Kama with his eye, whose guru Murugan is, and his dance on the peacock for the gods.
1203.nuance: அடியார் மனம் சலிக்க ... அபராதம் வந்து கெட்ட பிணம்: the image seems to be the corpse of one who grieved the devotees, made the model for the death the poet wants for his own malas. சுத்த வெளியாகி, becoming pure space, names the goal. The first line has a corrupt glyph and the division of the opening clauses is uncertain.

1204.reading: The first half is the talk of mourners over a body: don't leave the corpse at the threshold, raise a tall bier before it rots, deck it, call the drummers, stop the weeping, lift it before it stinks; and the poet asks that on the day his kin carry him to the burning ground, Murugan come quickly on the peacock with the hunters' daughter to guard his life. The praise tells of the elephant seized by the crocodile in the pond and Vishnu who came on Garuda blowing the conch, the vel thrown against the demons, and the gods resettled in their golden land.
1204.nuance: As in 21 the confession is made through quoted speech: the kin's instructions over the body (எடுமின் யாக்கையை) show how quickly the person becomes a thing to be disposed of.

1205.reading: The poet says that, by the decree of Brahma, consort of the goddess of letters, he has taken every form of body again and again, born at the mouth of every womb and stumbling through the world for aeons he cannot count, and asks Murugan to grant that he not be born again. The praise names the hunter girl of the green millet field where the elephant came, Indra's world upheld, the guardian of the western land, and the vel hurled so that the sea turned to mud and Sura and the mountain to ash.
1205.nuance: அக்ஷர தேவி கோவின் விதிப்படி: birth is assigned by Brahma's writ, the lord of Sarasvati. The opening (அப்படி ஏழும் ஏழும் வகுத்து, அக்ரம் வியோம கோளகை) and the Sanskrit run of epithets in the praise are hard to divide.

1206.reading: The poet describes lovemaking with women whose eyes close and speech falters, and admits that alone he cannot give up the embrace, so asks for Murugan's young feet rich in compassion. The praise has Siva of Kailas, Indra of the thunderbolt, Brahma and Vishnu on Garuda who tears the serpent's hoods, and the vel buried in clouds, sky, sea, mountain and the demon's chest.
1206.nuance: தமியேனால் தவிரொணாது: the poet confesses he cannot leave it by his own strength, so the feet must be given.

1207.reading: The poet describes women who call young men, draw out a great deal of money, embrace them on beds and melt them, and says he is drained, his tongue dry, living in fear and shame; he asks Murugan to end this labour and give the feet that lead to release. The praise names Siva, whom even Vishnu could not reach, dancing the great dance, to whom Murugan gave the teaching that made his devotion overflow, and the vel that pierced Sura's chest and let the friendly survive.
1207.nuance: மிக்க காசு இழைத்து: money is named, the courtesan's trade. சுகத்தில் அத்தர் தாம் மிகுத்த பத்தி கூர் சுரக்க வித்தை தான் அருள்வோனே: Siva, the father, receives the teaching and overflows with devotion.

1208.reading: The poet, worn out by Kama who shoots the bud arrows from his sugarcane bow, calls himself a vessel at the door of women like Rambha and a wandering lecher who seeks breasts that plot death like Death himself, and asks Murugan to give him virtues and join him to the good anklets. The praise names Rama who burned Lanka with his monkey army and Krishna who in one chariot sided with Arjuna against the hundred, and the vel that split the hill of Sura.
1208.nuance: கூற்றெனக் கொலைசூழும் குயங்கள்: desire is again Death. Several runs in the praise (பெருங்குறோட்டைவிட்டு உறங்கு காற்றென) are obscure.

1209.reading: Calling his body a bundle of flesh and filth, the poet asks whether, failing to reach release and wearing himself out in union with women, he should be slandered by men on earth as a buffoon, a rogue and a loudmouth. The praise names the Lord who knocked Brahma, the potter of the Veda, on the forehead, and the Tamil verses with the tala beat that sent the Jains in their mats onto rows of sharp stakes, with the victorious vel and unfailing compassion.
1209.nuance: கலைதலை கெட்ட பாய்ச் சமணரை நட்ட கூர்க் கழுநிரை ... ஏற்றிய தாளக் கவிதை: Murugan is identified with Sambandar, whose Tamil hymns sent the Jains to the stake. குயவனை ... குட்டினால்: Brahma struck as a potter, the punishment in the story of Om, though Om is not named here.

1210.reading: The poet describes the embrace of women plainly, until reason fails and day and night are forgotten, and asks to be given Murugan's red feet so that, with supreme knowledge made clear and love rising, he may speak his praise. The praise names Siva whom Vishnu and Brahma could not find, Devayanai the daughter of the gods' king, Valli in love's play, and Murugan who enters the minds of those who daily think on his anklets and leave their sins.

1211.reading: The poet heaps names on himself, without conduct, witless, angry, an offender, base, unfit, carried away by desire, a sinner whose mind never gained the knowledge that says neither 'you' nor 'I', and asks Murugan not to think so of him but, with a mother's and father's grace, to grant great knowledge. The praise has the vel that dried the sea, fed the ghouls and sent the demons to Yama's city, and the Lord who, not shrinking when the hunter bathed him with water from his mouth and said 'eat this flesh', ate what he had tasted as nectar.
1211.nuance: நீ நான் எனாத அறிவு: the knowledge the poet lacks is non-dual. The hunter's mouth-water bath and tasted flesh are Kannappar's offering, usually told of Siva at Kalahasti; here the praise seems to give it to the Lord the song addresses. The first lines have a corrupt glyph and obscure words (விபாணதன், மாறாம காரிலெனையினி).

1212.reading: The poet, a devotee full of longing, asks whether he will set his heart's lotus as the flower, thread love through it, tie it on his tongue with art so that it spreads the fragrance of knowledge, with a pure mind as the singing bee, and so adorn Murugan's radiant feet with a garland of the flowers of the letters. The praise names the hunter girl of the forest, Devayanai of the great elephant, and the vel that brought down Sura, who came out of the fish-filled sea.
1212.nuance: மாத்ருகா புஷ்ப மாலை: the garland is made of the மாத்ருகா, the letters of the alphabet held to be mother-powers, so the song itself is the offering; heart, love, tongue and mind each become part of the garland.

1213.reading: The poet describes women who kindle desire, ask for cloth and money, sway their breasts and mimic peacocks and parrots, and lead a man by their foul passage, and asks whether the infatuation that torments him will not end. The praise names the peacock that seizes and shakes the serpent, Hari's nephew whose feet fill devotees' minds, the vel thrown at Sura who harmed the gods, and the lord who rejoices with the hunter girl in the golden land of the Ponni river.
1213.nuance: ஆடைப் பணத்தை எடு: the women's demand is quoted. பொனி நீர் பொற்புவி: the Ponni, the Kaveri, is named, a pointer to a Chola-country shrine though the song is filed among the general songs.

1214.reading: The poet describes women who bewitch with desire, whose minds seek money, who melt men's life, laugh with anyone in the street and make quarrels, with poison eyes, and asks whether he will stop walking to their doors. The praise is a litany of the Goddess, Uma, mother of the seas and seven worlds: yogi, jnani, supreme Brahmi, Neeli, Narani, the excellent one, Abhirami of the Veda, mountain creeper, Manonmani; Murugan is her son, dear to Siva and Brahma.
1214.nuance: காசு தேடு மனத்திகள்: money is named. The praise gives almost all its space to the Goddess's names, so Murugan is praised as அருள்பாலா, child of her grace.

1215.reading: When eyes of poison weep, drums beat, the bier is raised, kin stand apart and Yama's servants show the palm leaf saying 'the time has come, come' and carry off the life, the poet asks first to be given the awareness to think with love on the anklets that crush the life of lust and give knowledge. The praise names Saravana, Valli's devotee in disguise, the child who came in the reed-bed as son to the six, and the one who spoke the word of lived knowledge when his old father asked, saying 'Lord, praise'.
1215.nuance: நாத போற்றி என முது தாதை கேட்க அநுபவ ஞான வார்த்தை அருளிய: Siva as the old father asks and Murugan teaches, Om not named. காலமாச்சு வருக என ஓலை காட்டி: the summons is quoted. வியாழ கோத்ர is obscure.

1216.reading: The poet describes women standing in the street with garlands and thin cloth on their breasts, and asks that, not speaking even a little with them, he speak daily of Murugan's vel, his blue peacock, his six lotus faces and the two consorts on either side. The praise names him son of the Lord whom Brahma and Vishnu could not find, husband of the hunter girl, younger brother of the elephant-faced one, and the vel thrown at Sura's chest.
1216.nuance: உரையாதே ... உரையேனோ: the poet turns his speech from the women to the Lord; the plea is about what the tongue does.

links.note: Both picture Yama's palm-leaf summons with drums, the bier and wailing kin; 23 draws the lesson of sharing before it comes, 1215 asks instead for love of the anklets.
Both name the courtesan's want as money, not love: the Kural warns that the sweet words of women who desire wealth bring harm, and 1214 calls them women whose minds seek coins.

source_issues: 1203: corrupt glyph in பிண஧முடி (line 1); புர்முணும் (line 10) probably for புரமூணும்.
1211: corrupt glyph in மோகாச஡ணத (line 3); விபாணதன் and மாறாம காரிலெனையினி are obscure, possibly garbled.
1214: the glyph ஡ stands for ஊ in வாயிலு஡றல் (வாயிலூறல், line 7); initial உ split from its word (உ மையாயி).
1207: initial உ split from its word (உ ருக்கி, உ ழைக்கும்).
